name: Suomenlinna
label: Suomenlinna
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kuninkaanportti' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Kuninkaanportti' (way/298540981): middle (29 m across).

text.description:
Suomenlinna is a sea fortress spread across eight islands, about four kilometres south-east of Helsinki city centre. Building began in 1748 under the Swedish Crown, and it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1991. Today it is as much a picnic spot as a monument, with pastel buildings, grassy ramparts and stone walls meeting open water. That mix is why it photographs so well on a phone.

For the first photo, go to Kuninkaanportti (the King's Gate), on the southern tip of Kustaanmiekka. It is often described as the island's main symbol. From the seaward side, in front of the gate, you can frame the stone gateway against the sea, with the Latin inscription and coat of arms above the archway. It can be quieter here than you might expect for such a well-known view.

If you have time, two other views are worth adding. The dry dock looks down into its stone-walled basin, with the old wooden ship hull and ochre storehouses around it. The Great Courtyard has the pastel barracks and the statue of Augustin Ehrensvärd in the foreground.

The gate is a walk from the ferry, so allow time. Winter snow is not cleared on the outer fortifications, so wear sensible shoes in cold months. Drones are generally restricted on the island, and it is wise to keep to marked paths on the ramparts.
text.geographic_location: Suomenlinna is a district of Helsinki on a group of islands in the sea, about four kilometres south-east of the city centre. Kuninkaanportti stands on the southern tip of Kustaanmiekka, the island with the most fortifications.
text.directions_text: Suomenlinna is on islands, so take the ferry from Helsinki. From the ferry landing, the King's Gate is a walk across the island, so allow extra time. Check the official site before you go for ferry times. The phone icon on the map is about 500 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the gate against the sea. Switch to the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the inscription and coat of arms above the archway. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of sea and sky around the gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 500 m south-east of the subject, at Kuninkaanportti (the phone icon on the map), and face north-west. On the seaward side in front of the gate on the southern tip of Kustaanmiekka. From here the stone gateway sits against the sea, with the Latin inscription and coat of arms visible above the arch. The main fortress marker on the map lies to the north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the archway up with the vertical lines so the stonework stands straight. Keep the whole arch and the coat of arms in frame, with the sea behind. If you want an alternative afterwards, the dry dock and the Great Courtyard each make a good second picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sea or sky looks washed out. Take a few frames, as walkers may pass through the arch.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset is recommended. In summer, morning light is said to light up the inscription.

text.access_note: The gate is outdoors on a public part of the island and free to photograph, but check the official site before you go for ferry times and seasonal hours.
claims_not_in_sources: A bright sea and sky behind the gate can make the stonework look dark unless the exposure slider is lowered.
Other visitors may walk through the archway while you are photographing.
Gridlines help keep an archway looking straight in a phone photo.

name: Temppeliaukio Church (Rock Church)
label: Rock Church
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Temppeliaukio Church'.

text.description: Temppeliaukio Church, also called the Rock Church or Church of the Rock, sits in the Töölö district and is built straight into the granite bedrock of Temppeliaukio ("Temple Square"). Timo and Tuomo Suomalainen designed it, and it was completed in 1969. Rather than putting a building on top of the rocky hill, they dug the main hall out of the rock and left much of the stone showing, so the raw rock forms the interior walls. A copper-lined dome sits above, ringed by skylights that let daylight in. That mix of granite, copper and light is why it photographs so well, both as a rough rocky outcrop from outside and as a calm, round hall inside. The church seats about 750 people. It is still a working Lutheran parish church, used for services, weddings and concerts, and it is also one of Helsinki's principal tourist attractions, with a record 938,000 visitors in 2019. If you go inside, remember people are there to worship or listen to music, so keep your phone quiet, skip flash and be considerate when taking pictures of other visitors.
text.geographic_location: In the Töölö district of central Helsinki, on the rocky hill of Temppeliaukio Square, in the Etu-Töölö area.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. The church is in Töölö, Helsinki. The phone icon on the map is about 80 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the dome and the rock walls inside, and for the whole rocky hill from outside. Use the default lens (1x) for natural-looking views, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the copper and the texture of the granite.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 80 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. From here you can photograph the rocky setting and the church's surroundings in context, then walk about 1 minute north-east to the church itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon level. Outside, include some of the bare rock in the foreground to show how the church grows out of the hill. Inside, stand near the centre if you can and point the ultra-wide (0.5x) upwards so the ring of skylights and the dome form a circle. Hold the phone steady with both hands and keep people out of the edges of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Inside, the skylights can be much brighter than the rock walls. Tap on the rock to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright ring keeps its detail. Portrait mode is not needed here. Panorama works for the curve of the rock wall if you turn slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Bright daylight lights the interior through the skylights, so the middle of the day is usually a good choice for inside shots. For outside shots, softer morning or late-afternoon light is kinder to the rock. Early in the day is often quieter, but check opening times first.

text.access_note: This is an active place of worship and a visitor attraction, so visiting times and photography rules can change; check the official site before you go.

name: Helsinki Cathedral and Senate Square
label: Helsinki Cathedral
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Helsinki Cathedral'.

text.description: Helsinki Cathedral stands at Senate Square in Kruununhaka, and it is a major landmark of the city. It has a tall green dome with four smaller domes around it, and a pale neoclassical body with columns and pediments on each arm. Carl Ludvig Engel designed it as the high point of his Senate Square layout, with the smaller buildings around the square also his work. Building began in 1830 and the church was inaugurated on 15 February 1852. It was first a tribute to Emperor Nicholas I of Russia, and it kept the name St Nicholas's Church until 1917. Although it is often called the 'White Cathedral', it is actually painted in three very similar light greys. Larger-than-life zinc statues of the Twelve Apostles stand along the roofline, and they make good close-up subjects. Walk closer for details of the columns and statues. Look left and right of the steps: the left building is the bell tower and the right one is a chapel, and including both gives a balanced, symmetrical picture. Expect other visitors in your frame, especially in summer, so take a few shots and pick the clearest.
text.geographic_location: In the Kruununhaka neighbourhood in the centre of Helsinki, at Senate Square.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Kruununhaka in the centre of Helsinki, by taxi or hired scooter if you are coming from further away. Walk towards the green dome and the wide steps. The phone icon on the map is about 120 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole cathedral and its steps. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you stand closer and want the dome and steps in one frame. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the dome, the colonnade and the apostle statues on the roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 120 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line up the central axis of the building with the middle of the screen, so the symmetry is clear and the columns stay upright. Include the bell tower on the left and the chapel on the right to frame the steps. For a closer picture, zoom to 2x-5x and aim at the apostle statues against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pale façade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the light grey walls keep their detail and the sky does not turn white. Keep the phone level to avoid leaning verticals.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime, when the façade is evenly lit, gives clean detail. Early morning is usually quieter on the square. In the evening, try night mode if the building is lit, and hold the phone steady against something solid.

text.access_note: The cathedral is open to visitors through the year, but hours vary with services and events, and an admission fee is charged in the main summer season, so check the official site before you go.

name: Löyly sauna
label: Löyly
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Löyly' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Löyly' (way/625576876): middle (58 m across).

text.description:
Löyly is a public sauna, restaurant and bar on the Hernesaari shore, opened in 2016 and designed by Avanto Architects. It is easy to see why it gets photographed: the building is a sculptural shell of wooden slats that sits low against the open Baltic, so the wood, the water and the sky make a simple, strong picture. It was designed to blend into the park-like coastline, and its roof is shaped like a big outdoor auditorium that visitors can climb for views. Time magazine put it on its 2018 list of the World's 100 Greatest Places, and the architecture has won a long list of awards.

For a phone photo, start at the entrance steps on the waterfront side, where the slatted wall fills one side of the frame and the sea fills the other. Sunset is the time most people recommend. Keep the horizon level using the gridlines, and let the curve of the wooden cladding lead the eye across the picture. If you want the whole shape of the roof with the sea and city beyond, a higher, wider spot on the building gives a different view. The roof and some outdoor areas may have access rules, so check the official site before you go. Be polite with people sitting on the steps and wait for a gap rather than asking anyone to move.
text.geographic_location: Löyly is in Hernesaari, a former industrial area on Helsinki's sea shore, at Hernesaarenranta 4. It is about 2.5 km southwest of the city centre, right on the water.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is given for this spot, so start from the centre of Helsinki and head south-west towards the Hernesaari waterfront, about 2.5 km away. On foot it is a fairly long walk of about 2.5 km. Once you reach the building, walk round to the waterfront side facing the open sea and find the entrance steps. The phone icon on the map is about 35 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the main shot of the wooden cladding with the sea behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the full sweep of the building from close up, and keep it away from the edges of the frame where lines can bend. A 2x telephoto setting works well for picking out the pattern of the slats.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 35 m north-east of the subject, at Löyly (the phone icon on the map), and face south-west. From here you see the slatted cladding with the open Baltic behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line, with the curve of the wooden wall running into the frame from one side. For a different view, a higher spot on the roof gives a wider look at the wave-like roof with the sea and city beyond, if access is allowed on the day.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sea or the sky to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sunset colours do not wash out and the wood keeps its texture. Take a few frames in case people walk through.

text.access_note: Check on the day whether the outdoor areas are free. The sauna is a paid venue, and roof access is not confirmed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Helsinki Central Station
label: Central Station
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Helsinki Central Station'.
notes: Eliel Saarinen's station and its lantern carriers.

text.description:
Helsinki Central Station is the city's main railway terminus, and it is as much a landmark as a place to catch a train. The granite building was designed by Eliel Saarinen and opened in 1919. It is known for its tall clock tower and for the Lyhdynkantajat ("The Lantern Bearers"), the statues by Emil Wikström beside the main entrance. The BBC named it one of the world's most beautiful railway stations in 2013. Around 200,000 people pass through every day, so the building is rarely quiet.

It photographs well because the shapes are so strong: a solid stone facade, a tall central tower and the figures at the entrance, all in one frame. The main front faces Kaivokatu, with Railway Square to the east and Eliel Square to the west. For the statues, either walk closer or use the zoom. Keep the gridlines switched on so the tower stays upright rather than leaning. People will walk through your frame, so take a few shots and pick the one with the cleanest foreground. The interior is a working station, so take a quick look at the official site before planning any indoor photos.
text.geographic_location: In the city centre of Helsinki, in the Kluuvi district at Kaivokatu 1. It sits between Railway Square to the east and Eliel Square to the west.
text.directions_text: Make your way to the city centre of Helsinki and to Kaivokatu, the street the station's main front faces. Walk north from there and the station is straight ahead. The phone icon on the map is about 130 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade and tower. Switch to 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the Lantern Bearers statues and the clock tower. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you walk right up to the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 130 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. From here the full granite front, the clock tower and the entrance are all in view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the tower with a vertical line, with the phone held level so the building doesn't lean. Put the tower slightly off-centre and leave a little sky above it. Wait for a gap in the passers-by before shooting.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone facade to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a touch if the sky is bright, so the granite keeps its detail. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight shows the granite front clearly, and a clear day gives a clean sky behind the tower. After dark, night mode helps with low light. Early mornings tend to be quieter for people-free shots.

text.access_note: The station is a working transport hub, so check the official site before you go for anything beyond passing through.
claims_not_in_sources: The stand-here point is on the Kaivokatu side, south of the station, with a clear view of the main front.
From about 126 m away the default lens (1x) on most phones fits the whole facade and tower in one frame.
Daylight from the south falls on the main front around midday on clear days.
Early mornings are usually quieter than the rest of the day.

name: Uspenski Cathedral
label: Uspenski Cathedral
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Uspenski Cathedral'.

text.description:
Uspenski Cathedral is the main cathedral of the Orthodox Church of Finland and the largest Orthodox church in Northern Europe. It stands on a hillside on the Katajanokka peninsula, looking over the city, so it rises above you as you approach. That height and the sheer bulk of the building are what make it work for photos. Even a simple shot from the foot of the hill looks imposing.

A few facts help you tell the story in your pictures. The cathedral was designed by the Russian architect Aleksey Gornostayev, but it was built after his death, between 1862 and 1868, under Ivan Varnek. It was inaugurated on 25 October 1868. About 700,000 bricks were shipped in by barge from the Bomarsund Fortress, which had been demolished in the Crimean War. The building is dedicated to the Dormition of the Mother of God.

The phone icon on the map is about 20 m south-east of the subject. At that range the building will not fit in a normal frame, so use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) and tilt the phone upwards. Try to keep the phone level so the walls do not lean too much. For a tighter picture of the upper parts of the building, step back if there is room and use the telephoto lens (2x or more) instead. Allow time for people walking past, as the cathedral is busy with visitors.
text.geographic_location: Uspenski Cathedral is on a hillside on the Katajanokka peninsula in Helsinki, overlooking the city.
text.directions_text: From the city centre, head for the Katajanokka peninsula and look for the cathedral on its hillside. Exact routes depend on where you start, so follow the map. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to fit the cathedral in from this close range. Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details higher up, and the default lens (1x) for general views.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 20 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. You are close, so the cathedral will fill most of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up a vertical edge of the building with one of them. Keep the phone as upright as you can to limit the leaning effect, and leave a little sky above the top. For a detail shot, zoom in on the upper part of the building rather than walking closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the cathedral to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so bright sky does not wash out the detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters a large building better than harsh midday sun. Earlier in the day is also likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: The cathedral is a working place of worship; the surroundings are easy to photograph, but entry has an admission fee outside services and it is closed on Mondays, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning and late-afternoon light is usually softer than midday sun.
Earlier in the day is likely to be quieter at the cathedral.
The cathedral can be busy with passers-by and visitors.

name: Sibelius Monument
label: Sibelius Monument
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Sibelius Monument'.

text.description:
The Sibelius Monument is a public memorial to the Finnish composer Jean Sibelius, who died in 1957. The sculptor Eila Hiltunen called her design Passio Musicae. It was unveiled on 7 September 1967 in Sibelius Park. The main part is a wave-like cluster of 569 stainless steel pipes welded together. It measures about 8.5 by 10.5 by 6.5 metres and weighs 24 tonnes. Nearby is a second element, a relief portrait of Sibelius in his mid-forties, framed by three free-form shards.

It photographs well because the textured pipes catch light and shadow in different ways from every angle. You can also step inside the hollow of the cluster, which gives a very different view looking up through the pipes. Some people see an organ in it, others see birch woods or reeds on the shore. Wind, rain and even echoing voices can make the pipes sound.

For photos, take one wide shot of the whole sculpture, then move in for details such as the pipe ends, the textures and the portrait. Walk around the cluster before you choose your angle. If you want a sense of scale, ask a friend to stand beside the pipes or inside the hollow. The steel has not tarnished over time, so it stays bright and reflective, and you may need to adjust exposure to avoid glare.
text.geographic_location: The monument is in Sibelius Park in the Töölö district of Helsinki, on the shore of Humallahti.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so head for Sibelius Park in the Töölö district. Check a local journey planner for the best way to reach Sibelius Park. The monument is only a few steps away, about 16 m to the north-east. The phone icon on the map is about 15 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole pipe cluster and some sky into one shot, especially from close by. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the pipe ends and the portrait relief.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 15 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. Walk closer afterwards for detail shots and try stepping inside the hollow.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the sculpture off-centre, with open space around it to show its shape. Take a low shot from near the pipes, pointing up. Then use the telephoto lens to pick out repeating pipe patterns and the portrait relief. If someone stands next to it, portrait mode can help, but check the edges of the pipes, which are fine detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the steel to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if bright reflections wash out the pipes. Take a few shots at different exposures and keep the best one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the park is quieter, such as early morning or late afternoon. Softer or lower light usually shows the texture of the steel better than harsh midday sun.

text.access_note: The monument stands in Sibelius Park and is cared for by the Helsinki Art Museum; check the official site before you go for any local notices.

name: Market Square (Kauppatori)
label: Market Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kauppatori' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Kauppatori' (way/457948795): middle (245 m across).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Market Square, Helsinki'.

text.description: Kauppatori is a central waterfront square in Helsinki, at the eastern end of Esplanadi, with the sea to the south and Katajanokka to the east. It works well for photos because several layers sit in one view: market stalls close by, boats and ferries on the water behind, and the domes of Uspenski Cathedral rising beyond. From spring to autumn the stalls sell Finnish food and souvenirs, and there are outdoor cafés around the square, so there is usually something going on to photograph. The square was built in the 1800s on what had been the muddy bottom of a bay, where fishermen once sold their catch from boats at the piers. About twenty metres of old railway track is still set into the cobblestones, which makes a nice detail for a close-up. The Presidential Palace and City Hall are next door, and a year-round ferry to Suomenlinna leaves from here. For the classic view, stand across the square from the stalls and face the harbour side. Zoom in a little so the market, the harbour and the cathedral stack up in one frame. Mornings are a good choice, when the market is busy and the light is soft. Keep an eye on your snacks, because the seagulls here are bold enough to snatch food from your hand.
text.geographic_location: Kauppatori is in central Helsinki, at the eastern end of Esplanadi on the waterfront, with Katajanokka just to the east. The Presidential Palace and City Hall stand next to the square.
text.directions_text: No tram or Underground stop is listed for this spot, so head for the eastern end of Esplanadi in central Helsinki. The square meets the sea there. From the phone icon on the map it is about 2 minutes on foot to the middle of the square, heading east. The phone icon on the map is about 100 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the harbour and the cathedral domes closer to the stalls. Switch to the default lens (1x) for wider views of the whole square. The ultra-wide (0.5x) suits close-ups of a stall or the old track set in the cobbles.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 100 m west of the subject, in Kauppatori (the phone icon on the map), and face east. Walk onto the square, stand across from the stalls facing the harbour side, and you should see market stalls in the foreground with the harbour, ferries and the Uspenski Cathedral domes beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the stalls along the lower third, with the water in the middle and the cathedral domes at the top. Zoom in so the layers sit close together. If you want a different angle, the terrace by Uspenski Cathedral looks down across the harbour and rooftops to the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stalls or a ferry to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and the domes stay clear. Wipe your lens first, as sea air and busy crowds can leave smears.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Between 8 and 11 a.m. on days the market is open, when it is busy and the light is soft.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space and free to photograph; the cathedral's interior has set opening hours, so check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside.

name: Esplanadi Park
label: Esplanadi
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Esplanadinpuisto' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Esplanadinpuisto' (relation/20999637): middle (376 m across).

text.description: Esplanadi, known to locals as Espa, is a long, tree-lined park in the middle of downtown Helsinki, running between Erottaja square and the Market Square. It works well for phone photos because the layout is simple. A wide central promenade, flowerbeds, mature lime trees and benches all lead the eye towards the statue of Johan Ludvig Runeberg, Finland's national poet. The statue was made by his son, Walter Runeberg, and stands at the centre of the park. People strolling along the promenade give the frame life and a sense of scale. Esplanadi is a popular walking area. In 1827 Engels Teater, the first theatre building in Helsinki, was put up in one corner of it. Street performances are often held here, and the park also hosts summer concerts and the Vappu (May Day) crowds. On those days people may block the classic view, so be ready to shoot from a slightly different angle or come back later. For the classic picture, stand in the middle of the park and face the monument from across the path, with trees on both sides to frame it. Take a few frames at different heights and zoom levels, and wait a moment for a clear gap in the crowd. If you have time, the seaward end of the park by the Havis Amanda fountain gives a different view with the waterfront behind.
text.geographic_location: Esplanadi is an urban park in downtown Helsinki, between Erottaja square and the Market Square. It lies between the Pohjoisesplanadi and Eteläesplanadi streets, with Stockmann and Hotel Kämp along its edge.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for downtown Helsinki and aim for Erottaja square or the Market Square at either end of the park. The phone icon on the map is on the western side of the park. The centre of Esplanadi and the Runeberg statue are about 159 m to the east, roughly a 2-minute walk along the promenade. The phone icon on the map is about 160 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the statue framed by trees and flowerbeds. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the full length of the promenade, or to the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick the statue out and flatten the busy background.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 160 m west of the subject, in Esplanadinpuisto (the phone icon on the map), and face east. Stand on the path opposite the Runeberg monument and face it across the path, with the promenade and its walkers behind the statue.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the statue slightly off-centre, with lime trees on both sides and a strip of flowerbed in the foreground. Turn on gridlines to keep the trees upright and the horizon level. If you want a second view, walk to the seaward end of the park for Havis Amanda with the waterfront and harbour light behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the statue to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the bronze keeps its detail. Try a Live Photo to catch people moving along the promenade, then choose the best frame.

text.description:
The SkyWheel and the Allas Sea Pool sit side by side on Helsinki's harbour edge, and together they make one of the more recognisable waterfront scenes in the city. The wheel rises beside the wooden pool terrace, with the harbour and ferries moving behind it. That mix of big round shape, warm timber and open water gives you plenty to work with on a phone.

For this spot we suggest stepping back to the Market Square (Kauppatori) waterfront rather than going in close. From there you see the wheel and the pool across the harbour, with Uspenski Cathedral nearby, so the picture says 'Helsinki' rather than just 'a Ferris wheel'. It is a wider, more contextual view than the close-up terrace.

The Allas terrace belongs to a paid sea-pool and restaurant complex, and we could not confirm whether the terrace can be reached without a spa ticket, so check on arrival. If you do go in, photos inside the pool area may only be allowed when no other people are in the frame, so the terrace and the square are the safest places to take pictures.

Start with a wide shot that includes some water in the foreground, then take a tighter frame of the wheel and pool alone. Check that the horizon looks level before you press the shutter.

text.description:
The Old Market Hall is the oldest market hall in Helsinki, and it still looks the part: a red brick building with a structure of cast iron, designed by Gustaf Nyström and opened in 1889, when Finland was a Grand Duchy. It stands on Eteläranta, right by the Market Square in the Kaartinkaupunki district, so the harbour is close by. It was last renovated between 2012 and 2014, when the hall closed for a year and a half.

The best photo is taken from the square, looking back at the hall's front and stalls. The brick gives you warm colour and strong texture. The market activity in front adds life, and the harbour behind helps place the scene. With a little zoom, Uspenski Cathedral can be seen rising in the distance, stacked behind the hall's busy front. If you have time, a second option is the South Harbour waterfront, where you can look along the hall's side and facade with the Market Square area in front of it.

Keep the phone level so the walls stay straight, and use the gridlines to line up the roof edge. Wait for a gap in the crowd if you want a cleaner frame, or include people and stalls for atmosphere. Come back in the afternoon if you can, as a travel guide suggests the afternoon, when the harbour side of the building is in lower light.

text.description: The Kamppi Chapel, also called the Chapel of Silence, stands on Narinkka Square in the Kamppi neighbourhood. It is meant as a place to calm down and have a quiet moment in one of the busiest parts of Helsinki. That contrast is what makes it fun to photograph: a calm, simple building surrounded by city activity. It was built as part of the World Design Capital programme in 2012 and designed by Kimmo Lintula, Niko Sirola and Mikko Summanen of K2S Architects. It won an International Architecture Awards prize in 2010. It proved popular straight away, with some 250,000 visitors by January 2013 and its 500,000th a year later. The chapel welcomes everyone, whatever their religion or background, and its design is deliberately plain and neutral. For your photos, start with the whole building from the square, then move closer for details of the walls and the entrance. Keep people in the frame if you like, as they show the scale and the busy setting. If you go inside, remember it is a place for quiet. Keep your phone silent, be discreet and respect other visitors.

text.description:
Katajanokka is the neighbourhood across the small canal from Helsinki's Market Square. It began as a headland, but a small canal dug across its base in the 19th century made it technically an island. Four bridges link it to the Market Square and Aleksanterinkatu side. That gives you a simple scene: water, bridges and the district rising beyond.

The south side is a busy passenger harbour, where large cruiseferries come and go on routes to Stockholm, Mariehamn, Tallinn and Rostock. The northern shore is a base for the coast guard, the maritime police and the Finnish icebreaker fleet, so there is often something working on the water. The older western part of the district is known for early 20th century Art Nouveau buildings. The Uspenski Cathedral (architect Alexey Gornostaev, 1868) is one of the district's best-known landmarks.

For a phone photo, use the water as your foreground and let the harbour and buildings fill the middle distance. Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon level, because straight quay edges and bridges look odd when they tilt. A ferry at the quay gives a strong sense of scale, but they are large, so step back or switch to the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to fit one in. Take a few frames as boats move through, and pick the one with the cleanest gap between objects.

text.description: The Ateneum is an art museum on the south side of Rautatientori square, right by Helsinki Central railway station. It is one of the three museums that make up the Finnish National Gallery and holds the largest collection of classical art in Finland. The building was designed by Theodor Höijer and finished in 1887, and its front is full of detail that rewards a closer look. Above the main entrance are busts of Bramante, Raphael and Phidias. Higher up, four caryatids hold up the pediment, and at the top Pallas Athene, the goddess of art, blesses the different art forms. Sixteen small medallion reliefs sit between the second-floor windows. Inside, the collection includes a Van Gogh painting that arrived in 1903, which made the museum the first in the world to have one. The phone icon on the map is about 95 m north-east of the subject. That shows the scale of the building, and you can then move in on the sculpture. Wait for a gap between passers-by if you want a clean frame. text.description: Kiasma is Helsinki's museum of contemporary art, on Mannerheimintie, and it looks every bit the modern building it is. It was designed by the American architect Steven Holl. His winning entry, called Chiasma, was chosen from 516 submissions in a competition decided in 1993. The Finnish form of that name gives the museum its title. Building began in 1996 and the doors opened in May 1998. The design was controversial at the time, partly because it stands so close to the equestrian statue of Mannerheim. That closeness is useful for photographers, because the old statue and the newer building can share a frame and tell a small story about the city. The museum is part of the Finnish National Gallery and looks after its contemporary collection. It closed for repairs in September 2014 and reopened in March 2015. Visitor numbers passed 310,000 in 2016. Start wide to take in the whole front, then move in for details of the walls and edges. Stand square on and use the gridlines to keep verticals straight. Walk a little to either side to find a diagonal view that gives the shot more depth. Keep people in the frame if you want a sense of scale.

text.description:
Parliament House is the seat of the Parliament of Finland, and it is one of the easiest big buildings in Helsinki to photograph because the front is so orderly. A row of fourteen tall red granite columns, from Kalvola, runs along the façade. Architect Johan Sigfrid Sirén designed it in a stripped classical style that mixes Neoclassicism with early twentieth-century modernism, so the columns are simple and the walls are clean and flat. That gives you strong vertical lines and a calm, symmetrical picture.

The building went up between 1926 and 1931 and was officially opened on 7 March 1931. It stands on Arkadianmäki, a hill beside Mannerheimintie, in the district of Etu-Töölö. On the lawn in front are statues of two former presidents, Kaarlo Juho Ståhlberg and Pehr Evind Svinhufvud, both carved by Wäinö Aaltonen. They make useful foreground details and show how large the building is. The Parliament Park lies just to the north.

Keep the phone level so the columns stay straight, and use the gridlines to line up the façade. Take one wide shot of the whole front, then a closer one of the columns and the statues.

text.description: The Finnish National Theatre stands on the north side of Helsinki's railway station square, and it is one of the best-looking buildings in the city centre. The granite facade was designed by Onni Tarjanne in the National Romantic style and finished in 1902. That was the year the company, founded in 1872 as a touring group, finally got a permanent home. It is the oldest professional theatre in Finland that performs in Finnish. In front of the main entrance is the memorial to the writer Aleksis Kivi, by Wäinö Aaltonen, put up in 1939. The statue is what makes the photo: it gives you a figure in the foreground and the heavy stone building behind it. The square is open, so you can step back far enough to fit the whole front in one frame. Take a first shot with the statue and facade together, then move in for a closer one of the stonework or the entrance. Stand a little off-centre so people crossing the square do not block the statue. Keep the phone level so the vertical lines of the facade do not lean. If the square is set up differently from usual, for example with a winter ice rink, check the foreground before you shoot. The theatre is a working building with performances, so for anything beyond the exterior, check the official site before you go.

shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime, when the facade is evenly lit, is the easiest. Early morning gives you fewer people crossing the square. In the evening, switch on night mode and hold the phone steady against something solid.

text.access_note: The square and the statue are open public outdoor space; for performances or going inside the theatre, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The theatre's front faces the square to the south, so the facade is usually well lit in daytime.
Early morning is usually quieter on the square than later in the day.
In winter there may be an ice rink or other seasonal set-up on the square that changes the foreground.
